extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of narrative theory; literary critics; creative writers studying narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Identify and analyze how narrative frequency (iteration) is constructed and varied in prose narrative — including pseudo-iteration, laws of recurrence, internal determination/specification, and the extension of iterative units. Useful for close reading, narratological analysis, or applying iterative techniques in creative writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-iterative
rubrics_metrics.description: Scenes presented, particularly by their wording in the imperfect, as iterative, whereas their richness and precision of detail ensure that no reader can seriously believe they occur and reoccur in that manner; a literary convention that presumes a 'willing suspension of disbelief.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explained as a long-standing rhetorical figure (hyperbole/sample of repeated soliloquies). In classical narrative the pseudo-iterative is figurative; in Proust it often functions in an 'impossible literalness.' Examples: repeated long conversations (Leonie and Françoise every Sunday at Combray), Carrizales' monologue described as spoken 'not once but a hundred times.' Note: apparent tense 'slips' (singulative passé simple inside iterative passages) can signal an intoxication with iteration rather than mere drafting error.

rubrics_metrics.name: Iterative as synthetic narrating (frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every iterative narrative is a synthetic narrating of the events that occur and reoccur in the course of an iterative series composed of a certain number of singular units.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Series are defined by diachronic limits and rhythm of recurrence; the synthetic unit can cover varying diachronic extent (e.g., 'Sundays in the summer of 1890' vs shorter iterations). Iterative narration tends toward abstraction if only invariants are kept, so internal diversification techniques are necessary for literary interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination (diachronic limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The series is defined first by its diachronic limits (determination) — its beginning and end — which can be explicit (dates) or by reference to singular events, or left implicit when recurrence is effectively unlimited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determination can be definite or indefinite ('starting from a certain year'). Examples: a breach between characters ending one series and starting another; literary texts often use singular events to mark determination. Determination can also punctuate stages and divide series into subsenses (subseries).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification (rhythm of recurrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification is the rhythm of recurrence that defines how often units of the series recur (e.g., every day, every Saturday, sometimes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifications can be indefinite (adverbs like sometimes) or definite (every day). There are simple specifications and complex specifications (superimposed laws, e.g., 'every Saturday in May'). Specifications may be used to create alternating variants (e.g., Meseglise way vs Guermantes way).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension (diachronic extent of constituent units)
rubrics_metrics.description: Extension is the diachronic length of each constituent unit of the series (how long one 'iterative unit' lasts in narrative time).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tiny iterations (e.g., 'every morning my alarm goes off') resist expansion; extended units (e.g., 'Sunday at Combray' or a sleepless night) provide enough material for narrative expansion. The extent chosen affects whether the iterative can be concretized or will remain diagrammatic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regularity / law of frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition should obey a law of frequency: the repetition must be regular, discernible, formulable, and therefore predictable in its effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proustian narrative displays an 'anxious search for a law of recurrence' (e.g., trying to determine if an absence happens every other day or on Saturdays). The feeling of soothing predictability comes from perceiving such a law; the narrator may gather observations to ascertain the rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal determination (singulative insertion determining subseries)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal determination: singulative events interposed into an iterative series that punctuate or divide the series into subseries, producing diachronic (before/after) variants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the breach between Swann and the Verdurins divides meetings into before/after subseries; the 'Lady in pink' meeting removes an earlier ritual and thus creates a before/after distinction. Internal determination arises from singulative segments and yields diachronically successive variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal specification (purely iterative subdivision/alternation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Internal specification is a technique of purely iterative diversification consisting of subdividing the recurrence to get alternating variants (not diachronically successive but alternating).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: dividing 'every day' into 'one day out of two' or alternating walk routes (Meseglise way/Guermantes way). Internal specification produces iterative variants that alternate rather than follow a before/after chronology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complex specifications / embedding of iterative units
rubrics_metrics.description: Complex specifications result when two or several laws of recurrence are superimposed or when iterative units are embedded in each other (e.g., every Saturday in May).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allows fine-grained control over recurrence patterns and can yield nested iterative structures; Combray shows multiple overlapping specifications (every year between Easter and October; every day/every Saturday/etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Concretization through internal determinations and specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: To avoid schematic barrenness when narrating iteration, the narrator uses internal determinations and specifications to 'concretize' the iterative series by introducing variants and internal detail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If only invariants are retained, narrative reduces to a timetable; diversification mechanisms (internal determination/specification) provide material for narrative expansion and reader interest (examples: different weather variants, anecdotal interpolations becoming ritual).

rubrics_metrics.name: Variants and their relations (diachronic vs iterative variants)
rubrics_metrics.description: Variants produced within an iterative series can be diachronic (subseries separated by singulative events) or iterative/alternating (specification-based variants).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diachronic variants arise from internal determination (before/after changes); iterative variants arise from specification (alternation, good-weather/bad-weather splits). The text demonstrates both kinds in daydreams and walk-route alternations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between determinative and non-determinative singulative episodes
rubrics_metrics.description: Not every singulative episode inserted into an iterative section determines a change; some are merely illustrations or exceptions without follow-up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysts must differentiate episodes that alter the series' course (determinative) from those that are isolated and leave the iteration intact (non-determinative). Example: the steeples of Martinville episode is not followed up and does not change the hero's customs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tense usage as marker of iterative vs singulative
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative tense can signal iteration or singulative aspect — the imperfect typically presents iteration, while the passé simple / passé composé can mark singulative events or paradoxically appear within iterative passages.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The imperfect lacks enough syntactic autonomy to begin an iteration in some constructions; paradoxical occurrences of singulative passé simple in iterative passages may reflect authorial 'intoxication' with iteration rather than textual error. Examples: 'je passai parfois' (I passed occasionally) and variants of the opening sentence written in passé composé vs passé simple.

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency locutions and their cataloguing (lexical markers of iteration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequentative locutions (certain days, other times, sometimes, often, most often) are lexical tools used to catalogue and present iterative variants as classes/types rather than isolated individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used stylistically to present a 'catalogue' of variants (e.g., portrait of Albertine as 'each of these Albertines' described through frequentative locutions). Cataloguing supports treating each occurrence as a type within a class, enabling rich iterative description.
